story.title: Walls that work for the city
story.lead: Apartment blocks across Central Asia have big walls that face the sun all day. Today those walls soak up summer heat and make no energy. SolarSkin turns them into small power plants that also shade the building.

method.title: How we count

items.p: A low-cost sensor kit reads power, sunlight and wall temperatures every minute. Nothing switches or controls the building.
One wall is shaded by the modules, the other is bare. The difference between them is the cooling effect.
CO₂ uses the UNFCCC grid factor (0.55 t/MWh). Anything we estimate is labelled as an estimate.

faq.title: Questions, answered
faq.lead: Everything you need to know about SolarSkin, in plain language.

items.a: A low-cost retrofit that mounts solar modules on the sunny walls of existing apartment blocks. The modules make electricity and shade the wall, so less summer heat gets into the building.

items.q: Does anything change inside the flats?
items.a: No. The modules are mounted on the outside wall, so nothing changes inside the flats and residents can stay at home during installation.

items.q: How much electricity will one wall make?
items.a: Our planning estimate for the 10 kWp pilot wall is about 8,000 kWh a year (800 kWh per kWp). Once the sensor kit is running, this dashboard will show the measured figure instead.

items.q: How do you know the wall is cooler?
items.a: We measure two walls: one shaded by the modules and an identical bare one on the same building. Temperature sensors on both show the difference every minute.

items.q: Can the system control anything in the building?
items.a: No. It is monitoring only: the sensor kit takes measurements and never switches or controls any equipment.
Not yet. The first SolarSkin wall will be installed and measured in Fergana. Until then, every figure on this page is labelled as a planning estimate.
